 New AARP study examines Social Security cuts risk and payroll-tax gap
 by 
 The FINANCIAL 
 November 13, 2026 
 in 
 America , Personal finance 
 Reading Time: 6 mins read
 8 
 0 
 A 
 A 
 A 
 A 
 Reset 
 0 
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 
 A new AARP study examining the risk of Social Security cuts estimates that the program could have paid full benefits until 2059 if the share of the economy subject to its payroll tax had held steady. The research, published November 10, measures how changing income patterns have reduced the program’s revenue base.
 The official financing deadlines remain earlier. Federal trustees project that retirement and survivors reserves will be exhausted in late 2032, while a hypothetical combination of the retirement and disability funds would last until 2034. Those estimates describe future financing under current law; they do not announce a new reduction in current payments.
 AARP measures a smaller taxable share of the economy
 The AARP Public Policy Institute’s summary puts earnings subject to the payroll tax at 34% of gross domestic product in 2025, down from roughly 41% in the early 1980s. Richard W. Johnson, the institute’s vice president of financial security, authored the research using Social Security Administration and Bureau of Economic Analysis data .

 AARP estimates an additional $10.8 trillion in revenue over 1984–2034 under its alternative scenario, extending full-benefit financing by 25 years from the combined funds’ projected 2034 deadline. That calculation describes a different historical revenue path. It does not identify an existing account containing that money or a legislated extension to 2059.
 In independent coverage published November 12 , Realtor.com reported that labor compensation’s share of GDP fell from 65% in 1970 to 57% in 2023. The report described how a greater share of income going to business profits and investment returns limits the growth captured by a payroll-based financing system.
 Realtor.com also reported AARP’s finding that taxpayers with incomes of at least $1 million accounted for 1% of filers in 2023 while receiving 48% of investment income. The publication attributed those figures to AARP’s analysis of Internal Revenue Service data .
 In its account of the research , AARP said gains in wages have been concentrated among high earners whose pay exceeds the taxable ceiling. It also identified investment returns and corporate profits growing faster than employee compensation. AARP advocates protecting benefits from cuts and presents expanding the revenue base as a policy option.
 How the wage ceiling limits collections
 For 2026, employees pay Social Security tax of 6.2% on earnings up to $184,500, according to the agency’s tax and benefit fact sheet . Employers pay a matching Social Security contribution. The applicable earnings ceiling rises to $192,300 in 2027, while the employee Social Security rate remains 6.2%.
 Medicare has a different tax base. Its regular employee rate is 1.45%, with no earnings ceiling, and additional Medicare tax applies above specified high-income thresholds. The commonly quoted 7.65% employee payroll-tax rate combines the regular Social Security and Medicare portions; it is larger than the Social Security rate alone.
 See also   Coachella 2027 names Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA as headliners The FINANCIAL previously examined the debate over raising or eliminating the payroll-tax cap . Under the existing structure, the ceiling also limits annual earnings counted in calculating benefits. Proposals to tax more earnings can differ over whether the additional wages would generate additional benefit credits.
 Retirement reserves and combined reserves have different deadlines
 The 2026 trustees report projects depletion of the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund in the fourth quarter of 2032. Continuing income would then cover 78% of scheduled benefits. The remaining 22% is the projected financing shortfall for that fund at depletion.
 The Disability Insurance Trust Fund has a stronger projected position, with reserves remaining positive throughout the report’s 75-year horizon. On a combined OASDI basis, the projected depletion date is the third quarter of 2034, when income would cover 83% of scheduled benefits.
 The funds are legally separate. The trustees’ summary of their findings explicitly describes the 2034 calculation as what would happen if the two funds were combined. Current law also prevents the programs from paying benefits beyond available income and reserves, and they cannot borrow.
 Payroll-tax collections would continue after reserves were exhausted. The trustees’ projected percentages therefore describe the portion of scheduled benefits that continuing income could finance. Exhaustion of accumulated reserves would leave insufficient financing for full payments, rather than eliminate all incoming revenue.
 The latest annual accounts show reserves declining
 The Social Security Administration’s June 9 release accompanying the trustees report put combined 2025 income at about $1.45 trillion and expenditures at about $1.61 trillion. Reserves fell by $160 billion during the year to approximately $2.56 trillion.
 Payroll-tax contributions supplied about $1.32 trillion of that income. Income taxation of benefits contributed another $58 billion, while interest provided $69 billion. Social Security paid approximately $1.60 trillion in benefits during 2025 and had 70 million beneficiaries at year-end.
 An estimated 185 million people worked in jobs covered by Social Security and paid payroll taxes in 2025. Administrative costs were $7 billion, or 0.4% of expenditures. The agency said total program costs had exceeded total income since 2021, with non-interest income falling below costs since 2010.
 The agency describes Social Security as largely a pay-as-you-go system, with current workers’ payroll taxes financing most benefits paid to current recipients. Accumulated reserves are invested in government bonds. Interest on those holdings accounted for 4.8% of program income in 2025, according to its statistical overview.
 Demographic assumptions remain part of the forecast
 The agency’s 2026 statistical overview projects about 60% more retired-worker beneficiaries over the next 50 years. Its rounded figures show the number of workers paying Social Security taxes per beneficiary falling from 2.6 in 2025 to 2.3 in 2035.
 See also   How to Get an Austrian Tax Refund as an Immigrant or Foreign Worker Trustees assess demographic, economic and program assumptions each year. Their calculations incorporate birth and death rates, immigration, employment, retirement patterns, wages, productivity, inflation and interest rates. The size of the covered workforce and its earnings affect revenue alongside the number of people receiving benefits.
 The headline projections use the trustees’ intermediate assumptions, which they describe as their best estimates. The report also supplies low-cost and high-cost scenarios to illustrate uncertainty. Trustees review their assumptions as new information becomes available, so the forecast is not a fixed prediction of the exact date or size of a future payment change.
 In their annual summary, the trustees recommended that lawmakers address financing shortfalls in time to introduce changes gradually. They said earlier action would give workers and beneficiaries more time to prepare and allow the revenue increases or benefit reductions required to be shared across more generations.
 AARP’s discussion of the new research identifies proposals to collect more from high earners, including changing the wage ceiling and taxing some investment income. These are proposals for changing the financing system. The current taxable maximum and the official reserve projections remain the published benchmarks.
 Benefits already announced for 2027
 For the coming year, Social Security has announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment , beginning with benefits payable in January 2027 to nearly 72 million beneficiaries. Higher Supplemental Security Income payments begin December 31, 2026, for about 7.3 million recipients. Some people receive payments from both programs.
 The agency estimates that the average monthly retired-worker benefit will rise from $2,095 before the adjustment to $2,170 afterward. Those are program averages, rather than amounts promised to every retiree. Individual benefits depend on the applicable earnings record and benefit calculation.
 Frequently asked questions
 Does the AARP study move Social Security’s funding deadline to 2059?
 No. It examines an alternative history of the program’s revenue base. AARP describes the extra financing as what Social Security could have collected if changing income patterns had not reduced the share of the economy supporting payroll-tax revenue. The study does not change the law.
 Why do projections cite both 2032 and 2034?
 The earlier date applies to retirement and survivors reserves. The later date combines those reserves with disability reserves for illustration. Their projected payable-benefit percentages at depletion are 78% and 83%, respectively; the two dates refer to different financing pools.
 Are the projected cuts the change announced for January 2027?
 No. The change announced for January is a 3.6% cost-of-living increase in Social Security benefits. The financing shortfalls described in the trustees report concern later years. The agency’s announced adjustment and the long-term reserve projections address separate parts of the program.
